strings.title: Whole Numbers Times Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To multiply a whole number by a fraction, find one part first (divide by the denominator), then take as many parts as the numerator says.
strings.keywords: of, unit fraction, one part, numerator, denominator, bar model
watchFor: Multiplying the whole number by the denominator (12 × 3/4 = 48/4 and stopping): ask "Is 3/4 of 12 more or less than 12?"
Dividing by the numerator instead of the denominator: ask "How many equal parts is the bar split into?"
Thinking the answer should be bigger than the whole number: ask "What is 1/2 of 20?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 1/4 of 20 help with 3/4 of 20?" Land: find one part by dividing by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 12 × 3/4 and 3/4 of 12 are the same.

problems.notes: Look for: 20 split into 4 equal parts. Ask: "How big is one part?" Word choice: "one fourth of". Model: bar 1/4 of 20

responses.tip: One part first.

responses.say: Half of 20 is 10, half of that is 5.

problems.notes: Look for: three of those parts. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: bar 3/4 of 20

responses.say: One fourth is 5, so three fourths is 15.
responses.tip: The target strategy.
Whole minus one part. Clever.
Ask: is three quarters of 20 more or less than 20?

problems.notes: Look for: one fifth is 6, two fifths is 12. Ask: "What's one part?" Model: bar 2/5 of 30

responses.say: A fifth of 30 is 6, two fifths is 12.

responses.tip: Divided by the numerator. Ask: how many equal parts does the bar have?

problems.notes: Look for: the same as 3/4 of 12. Ask: "Is 12 × 3/4 the same as 3/4 of 12?" Model: bar 3/4 of 12

responses.say: 3/4 of 12: one fourth is 3, three fourths is 9.
responses.tip: Ask: why can we switch it to 3/4 of 12?
Multiply first, then divide. Same answer.
Forgot the fourths. Ask: should 12 × 3/4 be bigger than 12?

problems.notes: Look for: a third of 15 is 5, two thirds is 10. Ask: "Which is easier: divide first, or multiply first?" Model: bar 2/3 of 15

responses.say: A third of 15 is 5, two thirds is 10.

problems.notes: Look for: an eighth of 24 is 3, five eighths is 15. Ask: "What's one eighth?" Model: bar 5/8 of 24

responses.say: An eighth of 24 is 3, so 5 eighths is 15.
Half of 24 is 12, plus one more eighth (3) is 15.
responses.tip: 5/8 as a half and an eighth.
Divided by the numerator. Ask: what does the 8 tell us?

problems.notes: Look for: an eighth of 40 is 5, three eighths is 15. Ask: "What do you notice about the last two answers?" Model: bar 3/8 of 40

responses.say: An eighth of 40 is 5, three eighths is 15.

strings.title: Dividing Whole Numbers by Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing a whole number by a fraction asks how many of those fractions fit. Count how many unit fractions fit, then group them: 4 ÷ 2/3 is 12 thirds in groups of 2, which is 6.
strings.keywords: how many fit, unit fraction, groups of, number line, measure
watchFor: Expecting the answer to be smaller than the whole number: ask "How many halves fit in 2?"
Stopping at the unit fraction count (4 ÷ 2/3 = 12): ask "How many thirds are in one 2/3?"
Multiplying instead (6 × 3/4 = 4 1/2): ask "Are we finding a part of 6, or how many 3/4s fit?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 4 ÷ 1/3 help with 4 ÷ 2/3?" Land: count how many unit fractions fit (multiply by the denominator), then put them into groups (divide by the numerator).

problems.notes: Look for: 2 halves in each whole. Ask: "How many halves fit in 2?" Word choice: "how many 1/2s fit in 2". Model: numberline 0 +1/2x4

responses.tip: Found half of 2. Ask: how many halves fit in 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 thirds per whole, 4 wholes. Ask: "Hold on to this one." Model: numberline 0 +1/3x12

responses.tip: Hold on to this.

problems.notes: Look for: 12 thirds in groups of 2. Ask: "How does 4 ÷ 1/3 help?" Model: numberline 0 +2/3x6

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Counted thirds, not two-thirds. Ask: how many thirds in one 2/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 24 fourths in groups of 3. Ask: "How many fourths in 6?" Model: numberline 0 +3/4x8

responses.tip: Multiplied. Ask: are we finding 3/4 of 6, or how many 3/4s fit?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 fifths in groups of 3. Ask: "What's the same as the last one?" Model: numberline 0 +3/5x5
Context: "5 m of ribbon, cut into 1/2 m pieces." Look for: 2 pieces per metre. Ask: "How many pieces?" Model: numberline 0 +1/2x10

responses.tip: Ask: can cutting 5 m into half-metres give only 2 1/2 pieces?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 fifths in groups of 2 is 7 groups, with 1 fifth left (half a group). Ask: "What do we do with the leftover fifth?" Model: numberline 0 +2/5x7 +1/5

responses.say: 7 jumps of 2/5 is 2 4/5, and the last 1/5 is half a jump: 7 1/2.
responses.tip: Ask: why half a jump?
Named the leftover in fifths. Ask: what part of a 2/5 jump is 1/5?

strings.title: Fifths and Tenths
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Halves, fifths and tenths all fit together because tenths are the common piece: 1/2 = 5/10 and 1/5 = 2/10.
strings.keywords: common denominator, equivalent fractions, tenths, fifths, halves, rename
watchFor: Adding tops and bottoms (1/2 + 3/10 = 4/12): ask "Is 4/12 more than 1/2?"
Renaming 2/5 as 2/10: ask "How many tenths are in one fifth?"
Forgetting to simplify 8/10: ask "Can you name 8/10 with fifths?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why are tenths so useful here?" Land: a half is 5 tenths and a fifth is 2 tenths, so tenths are a common piece. Rename, then add or subtract the tenths.

problems.notes: Look for: 5/10 + 3/10 = 8/10 = 4/5. Ask: "How many tenths is a half?" Word choice: "same-sized pieces". Model: numberline 0 +1/2 +3/10

responses.tip: Ask: why does 8/10 equal 4/5?
Decimals are tenths too.
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 4/12 more than 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 4/10 + 3/10. Ask: "How many tenths in 2/5?" Model: numberline 0 +2/5 +3/10

responses.tip: Renamed 2/5 as 2/10. Ask: how many tenths in one fifth?

problems.notes: Look for: 6/10 + 5/10 = 11/10. Ask: "Is it more than 1?" Model: numberline 3/5 +2/5 +1/10

responses.tip: Make a whole.

problems.notes: Look for: 10/10 − 3/10. Ask: "How many tenths in 1?" Model: numberline 1 -3/10
Look for: 8/10 − 5/10. Ask: "How does the first problem help?" Model: numberline 1/2 >4/5

responses.say: From 1/2 up to 4/5 is 3/10, just like the first problem.

responses.tip: Subtracted tops and bottoms. Ask: is the answer really 1?

problems.notes: Look for: back 2/10 to 2, then 5/10 more to 1 1/2. Ask: "Can you go through the whole number?" Model: numberline 2 1/5 -1/5 -1/2

strings.title: Count Up to Subtract Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Subtract fractions with different denominators by counting up: from the smaller number to the next whole, then to the bigger number. Then add the jumps, using a common denominator.
strings.keywords: count up, next whole number, common denominator, unlike denominators, mixed numbers
watchFor: Subtracting tops and bottoms: ask "Are the pieces the same size?"
Getting stuck renaming 2 1/4 to take away 2/3: ask "How far is 2/3 from 1? From 1 to 2 1/4?"
Adding the jumps without a common denominator (1/3 + 1 1/4 = 1 2/7): ask "What size pieces can show thirds and quarters?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does counting up avoid the hardest part?" Land: jumping to the next whole number means you never take a big fraction from a small one. Add the jumps at the end with a common denominator.

problems.notes: Look for: 2/3 up 1/3 to 1. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 2/3 >1
Look for: 1/3 to 1, then 1 1/4 more: 1/3 + 1 1/4 = 1 7/12. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "count up to the whole". Model: numberline 2/3 >1 >2 1/4

responses.tip: The target strategy.

responses.say: On the clock: 135 minutes − 40 minutes = 95 minutes.
responses.tip: Minutes are twelfths: 95 minutes is 1 7/12 hours.
Added tops and bottoms of the jumps. Ask: what size pieces show thirds and quarters?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/4 to 2, then 1 1/2. Ask: "What's the next whole after 1 3/4?" Model: numberline 1 3/4 >2 >3 1/2

responses.tip: Took 1/2 from 3/4 the wrong way. Ask: should the answer be less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/6 to 1, then 1 1/3: 1/6 + 1 2/6 = 1 3/6. Ask: "Can you simplify 3/6?" Model: numberline 5/6 >1 >2 1/3
Look for: 1/2 to 3, then 1 1/5: 5/10 + 1 2/10. Ask: "What common piece works for halves and fifths?" Model: numberline 2 1/2 >3 >4 1/5

responses.tip: Decimals: also tenths.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/4 to 4, then 1 1/6: 3/12 + 1 2/12. Ask: "Which jumps?" Model: numberline 3 3/4 >4 >5 1/6
Look for: 1/2 to 4, then 2 1/8. Ask: "Is it the same pattern?" Model: numberline 3 1/2 >4 >6 1/8

strings.title: Fractions or Decimals?
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Some problems mix fractions and decimals. Change one so they match, using the equivalents you know: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/5 = 0.6, 1/8 = 0.125.
strings.keywords: fraction, decimal, equivalent, half, quarter, fifth, eighth, convert
watchFor: Adding a fraction and a decimal as they're written (0.75 − 1/2 = 0.73): ask "What is 1/2 as a decimal?"
Mixing up 3/5 and 0.35: ask "How many tenths is 3/5?"
Not knowing 1/8 = 0.125: ask "What's half of 0.25?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you decide which form to use?" Land: change one so both match, using the equivalents you know. Fractions are easier for thirds; decimals for tenths and hundredths.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/2 = 0.5, so 0.75 − 0.5. Ask: "What is 1/2 as a decimal?" Word choice: "equivalent". Model: numberline 0.5 >0.75

responses.tip: As fractions.
Read 1/2 as 0.02. Ask: what is half as a decimal?

problems.notes: Look for: 1.5 − 0.6. Ask: "Which form is easier here?" Model: numberline 0.6 >1 >1.5
Look for: 3/4 = 0.75, and 0.25 + 0.75 = 1. Ask: "What do you notice?" Model: numberline 2.25 +0.75

responses.tip: Partners: 1/4 and 3/4.

problems.notes: Look for: 3/5 = 0.6. Ask: "How many tenths is 3/5?" Model: numberline 0.6 +0.15

responses.tip: Read 3/5 as 0.35. Ask: what is 1/5 as a decimal?

problems.notes: Look for: 5/8 to 2, then 2 more. Or 4 − 1.375 = 2.625. Ask: "Fractions or decimals?" Model: numberline 1 3/8 >2 >4

responses.tip: The same as 2 5/8.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/8 = 0.125. Ask: "What's half of 0.25?" Model: numberline 0.125 +0.375
Look for: 2.5 − 1.125, or 2 4/8 − 1 1/8 = 1 3/8. Ask: "Which way?" Model: numberline 1.125 >2 >2.5

strings.title: Fractions: Choose a Strategy
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Look at the fractions first: are they partners that make a whole? Close to a whole number? Do they need a common denominator? Then choose: make a whole, count up, or rename.
strings.keywords: make a whole, count up, common denominator, clock, rename, partners
watchFor: Renaming everything without looking first: ask "Do any of these make a whole?"
Taking a big fraction from a small one: ask "Could you count up instead?"
Forgetting to simplify: ask "Can you name 6/12 another way?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you decide what to do?" Land: partners make a whole; numbers near a whole suggest counting up or taking a whole and adding back; different denominators need same-sized pieces (the clock helps for halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, twelfths).

problems.notes: Look for: 3/4 + 1/4 = 1, plus 1/2. Ask: "What makes a whole?" Model: numberline 3/4 +1/4 +1/2
Look for: take 1/6 from one of the wholes. Ask: "How many sixths in a whole?" Model: numberline 2 -1/6

responses.tip: Ask: if you take 1/6 from a whole, how much of that whole is left?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/3 = 2/6, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6. Ask: "Same-sized pieces?" Model: clock 5/6 - 1/3

responses.tip: Subtracted tops and bottoms. Ask: can the answer be more than 5/6?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/2 to 2, then 1/6. Ask: "How do you split the 2/3?" Model: numberline 1 1/2 +1/2 +1/6
Look for: count up 1/4 to 3, 1/4 more. Ask: "Close together?" Model: numberline 2 3/4 >3 >3 1/4
Look for: 7/8 + 1/8 = 1, then 4/8. Ask: "What does 7/8 need?" Model: numberline 7/8 +1/8 +4/8

responses.tip: Added the denominators. Ask: is the answer more than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 7/12 to 3, then 1. Ask: "Which strategy?" Model: numberline 2 5/12 >3 >4

strings.title: Fractions of Whole Numbers: One Part First
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To find a fraction of a whole number, find one part first (divide by the denominator), then take as many parts as the numerator.
strings.keywords: fraction of, one part, unit fraction, numerator, denominator, bar model
watchFor: Dividing by the numerator (3/4 × 28 = 28 ÷ 3): ask "How many equal parts is the bar split into?"
Multiplying both parts (3/8 × 32 = 96/256): ask "Is 3/8 of 32 more or less than 32?"
Stopping at one part: ask "How many parts do we want?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why find one part first?" Land: the denominator tells how many equal parts; one part is the whole ÷ the denominator. Then the numerator tells how many parts to take.

problems.notes: Look for: a third of 18 is 6, two thirds is 12. Ask: "What's one part?" Word choice: "two thirds of 18". Model: bar 2/3 of 18

responses.tip: Divided by the numerator. Ask: how many equal parts?

problems.notes: Look for: a sixth is 3, five sixths is 15. Or 18 − 3. Ask: "Take away one part?" Model: bar 5/6 of 18

responses.tip: Whole minus one part.

problems.notes: Look for: a quarter is 7, three quarters is 21. Model: bar 3/4 of 28
Look for: an eighth is 4, three eighths is 12. Model: bar 3/8 of 32

responses.tip: Forgot the eighths. Ask: is 3/8 of 32 more or less than 32?

problems.notes: Look for: a tenth is 5, seven tenths is 35. Model: bar 7/10 of 50
Look for: a ninth is 3, four ninths is 12. Model: bar 4/9 of 27
Look for: a twelfth is 3, five twelfths is 15. Model: bar 5/12 of 36

strings.title: How Many Groups? Whole Numbers Divided by Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of those fractions fit. Count the unit fractions first (6 ÷ 1/3 = 18), then group them by the numerator (6 ÷ 2/3 = 18 ÷ 2 = 9).
strings.keywords: how many fit, groups, unit fraction, numerator, denominator, number line
watchFor: Stopping at the unit fractions (6 ÷ 2/3 = 18): ask "How many thirds are in one 2/3?"
Multiplying instead (9 × 3/4): ask "Are we finding 3/4 of 9, or how many 3/4s fit?"
Expecting a smaller answer: ask "How many 1/6s fit in 4? More or fewer than 4?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did the unit fraction help?" Land: count the unit fractions (whole × denominator), then put them in groups the size of the numerator.

problems.notes: Look for: 3 thirds per whole, 6 wholes. Ask: "Hold on to this." Word choice: "how many thirds fit in 6". Model: numberline 0 +1/3x18
Look for: 18 thirds in groups of 2. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 0 +2/3x9

responses.tip: Group the thirds.
Counted thirds, not two-thirds. Ask: how many thirds in one 2/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 36 fourths in groups of 3. Ask: "How many fourths in 9?" Model: numberline 0 +3/4x12

responses.tip: Multiplied. Ask: 3/4 of 9, or how many 3/4s fit in 9?

problems.notes: Look for: 50 fifths in groups of 2. Model: numberline 0 +2/5x25
Look for: 6 sixths per whole, 4 wholes. Model: numberline 0 +1/6x24
Look for: 30 sixths in groups of 5. Ask: "What do you notice?" Model: numberline 0 +5/6x6
Look for: 96 eighths in groups of 3. Model: text 12 ÷ 1/8 = 96 ; 96 ÷ 3 = 32
